title: A proof of the Brian\c{c}on-Iarrobino Conjecture in three dimensions: the upper bound for the tangent space (Theorem A)
author: Owen Mackenzie; Fatemeh Rezaee
work: A proof of the Brian\c{c}on-Iarrobino Conjecture in three dimensions
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the upper bound for the tangent space of the Hilbert scheme of points in three dimensions, printed as Theorem A (Upper bound) of the paper (native source0.tex lines 700--711), delivered together with the authors' own complete proof of it (source0.tex lines 1085--1119, a proof environment carrying the optional heading Proof of Theorem ref thm:upperbound and closed by the authors). Theorem A is the technical heart of the paper: with the monotonicity Theorem B it yields the three-dimensional Briancon-Iarrobino conjecture (the paper's Corollary 1), and the authors describe it as strengthening the previously known bound up to a factor 4/3 by Ramkumar-Sammartano through a new error term. Why the unit is research-level rather than an ordinary qualifying problem: the proof has to compare hom(I,R/I) with the sum of the graded pieces hom(I_i,S/I_j) and then subtract, for every pair i>j, the number binom(i-j,2) of maps that occur in a bounded connected component but cannot extend to the tangent space; establishing that those maps are exactly the zero vectors requires the paper's Lemma 2.1 (retained with its proof), which uses Borel-fixedness and a strictly negative x-exponent to force gamma + alpha + e_y and gamma + alpha + e_x out of the monomial ideal; the counting is then assembled with the two inequalities hom(J,S/J') <= l + l' - t(J,J') (the paper's Corollary 1.15, retained with the Section 1.6 machinery that defines the spaces A, B and the function t(J,J'), and the paper's Corollary 2.2, retained) and with the double-binomial identity sum_{j} sum_{i>j} binom(i-j,2) = binom(m_1+2,4) applied twice, producing T(I) <= (2m_1+1)l - 2 binom(m_1+2,4). Every one of those ingredients is a non-obvious reduction: the tangent space is decomposed into graded pieces whose individual dimensions exceed the total, the correction term has to be identified and counted, and the error term is what upgrades an upper bound that merely misses the conjecture by a constant factor into an exact one in three dimensions. H2.
